slides.title: Hair is hard
slides.speech: Peekaboo and Illusions steer pixels the model already makes. Transparency it can't make at all, it only outputs RGB, and Peekaboo's blobby masks showed that gap. This is an alpha matte: white is the object, black is background, every gray strand is partly see-through. To teach alpha you need data. Matting datasets are made by hand, so they stop at a few hundred objects; the largest general-purpose one has 726. Segmentation sets like COCO are huge, but their edges are hard traced outlines, no hair. So here the handle is data: can a frozen RGB model build a big alpha dataset for us?

slides.title: The trick
slides.speech: The trick is embarrassingly simple: ask for the object on a green screen, then chroma key it like Hollywood does. Why not run a matting network on generated images? Its mistakes would become our ground truth. With a flat screen the background color is known at every pixel, so the compositing equation, image equals alpha times foreground plus one minus alpha times background, is nearly solved, and we get spill-free foreground colors too. But pine needles on green: the key eats the needles. On blue, much better.

slides.title: Pick the screen
slides.speech: So we pick the screen color per prompt. Generate the plain prompt once with SDXL, take a hue histogram weighted by saturation, and choose the named color the object uses least. She's all reds and some blues, so she gets green. Over 90 percent of the dataset ends up green or blue.

slides.title: Keyable images
slides.speech: Catch is, SDXL, Midjourney and DALL-E make dark gradient screens or tint the subject green. DeepFloyd, left, gives a flat screen, but the hair is mush. So we chain them. Cut DeepFloyd's girl out roughly with Photoshop, paste her on brighter pure green, and run SDEdit, SDXL image-to-image, at strength 0.95. That repaints almost everything, so it's a new girl with real flyaway hair; DeepFloyd only donates the layout and a clean screen. And green goes in the negative prompt: it strips spill off the girl, but the screen is too bright and saturated to suppress.

slides.title: Three keyers

elements.text: Agreement is our proxy for correctness.

slides.speech: Keying is under-constrained, so we run three keyers that fail differently: a classic per-pixel color-difference keyer, where we get the background by deleting the object and inpainting the hole, so gradients are fine; Adobe's internal learned chroma-key network; and Photoshop subject select. Top row cutouts, bottom row alphas. The score composites each cutout on white and on black and takes the worst pairwise MS-SSIM. Right, all three agree, 0.995. Left, a glass of water, they don't. The top half by score, above the median 0.984, is auto-accepted with the pixel-wise keyer: 110,000 images. For 40,000 more, mostly glass and smoke, a human clicked the best of seven alpha and color combos.

slides.title: 150,000 cutouts

elements.text: Matting error (SAD): best mix 33, either set alone 36 / 65

slides.speech: That's MAGICK: 150,000 objects, each with foreground colors, an alpha matte and a caption. Each pair is the object on gray, then its alpha. It helps matting too: training a matting network on a mix of MAGICK and the real DIM set gets error 33 on the DIM test, versus 36 and 65 for either set alone. Thousands of downloads a month. Cost: 32 A100s for three weeks plus two months of annotation, about 30,000 dollars. Limits: it's synthetic, so a stop sign gets a perfect matte and misspelled text, and some mattes keep soft shadows.

slides.title: Alpha in, image out

elements.text: 52 raters preferred ours 82% vs Canny, 77% vs sketch

slides.speech: With that data we fine-tuned an SD1.5 ControlNet: you give it an alpha matte plus a prompt, and it paints a matching image. Left, the inverted alpha. Middle, ours: hair lands where the alpha says. Right, ControlNet's segmentation model ignores it. No prior model takes alpha, so in the user study we compared against Canny-edge and sketch-edge ControlNets on the same base, on 27 unseen alphamatting.com masks. 52 people picked the better set for looks and prompt fit. So now we control what's in a frame down to a single hair. But nothing yet controls how it moves over time. That's the next handle.
